title: Valid Parentheses — stack matching pairs.

s1_definition.profdef: The Valid Parentheses problem checks whether a string of brackets, round, square, and curly, is correctly balanced and properly nested. The stack solution pushes each opening bracket and, on each closing bracket, verifies the top of the stack is the matching opener and pops it, rejecting on any mismatch or empty stack, and finally requires the stack to be empty. It runs in linear time with stack space proportional to the nesting depth.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India validates nested grouping markers in a formula string used for fee calculations, where every opening bracket must be closed by the right kind in the right order. Imagine a stack of plates. Each time you see an opening bracket you put a plate on top. Each time you see a closing bracket, the plate on top must be its exact partner, and you remove it. If the top is the wrong kind, or there is no plate, the string is invalid, and at the end the stack must be empty.
s1_definition.oneliner: Push openers, and on each closer the stack top must be its exact match; the stack must end empty.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Valid Parentheses problem checks whether a string of brackets, round, square, and curly, is correctly balanced and properly nested. The stack solution pushes each opening bracket and, on each closing bracket, verifies the top of the stack is the matching opener and pops it, rejecting on any mismatch or empty stack, and finally requires the stack to be empty. It runs in linear time with stack space proportional to the nesting depth.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India validates nested grouping markers in a formula string used for fee calculations, where every opening bracket must be closed by the right kind in the right order. Imagine a stack of plates. Each time you see an opening bracket you put a plate on top. Each time you see a closing bracket, the plate on top must be its exact partner, and you remove it. If the top is the wrong kind, or there is no plate, the string is invalid, and at the end the stack must be empty.

**One line to remember:** Push openers, and on each closer the stack top must be its exact match; the stack must end empty.

sections.s2_technical:
Balanced brackets follow a last-opened-first-closed discipline, which is exactly what a stack models. You scan the string character by character. When you see an opening bracket, one of round, square, or curly, you push it onto the stack. When you see a closing bracket, you must check that the stack is not empty and that its top element is the corresponding opening bracket; if so, you pop the top, otherwise the string is invalid and you return false immediately.

The two failure conditions on a closer are both important. If the stack is empty when you meet a closer, there is no opener to match, so it is invalid, like closing a bracket that was never opened. If the stack top is a different kind of opener, the nesting is crossed, like opening a round bracket then trying to close it with a curly one, which is also invalid. Only when the top is the exact matching opener do you pop and continue.

After the whole string is scanned, you require the stack to be empty. A non-empty stack means some opening brackets were never closed, so the string is unbalanced even though no mismatch occurred during the scan. This final emptiness check is as essential as the per-closer checks; forgetting it would wrongly accept a string like a single opening bracket.

A senior point is using a map from each closing bracket to its expected opening bracket, which makes the matching logic clean and easy to extend to more bracket types. On a closing bracket you look up its expected opener and compare it to the popped or peeked top. This avoids a tangle of if-else comparisons and keeps the code readable and correct.

Another senior point is the early-exit efficiency and the odd-length shortcut. You return false the instant a mismatch or an empty-stack-on-closer occurs, so invalid strings often fail fast. A quick optimization is that a string of odd length can never be balanced, so you can reject it in constant time up front. For memory, the stack grows to at most the maximum nesting depth, which for deeply nested fee formulas is worth noting.

A small finance-domain example: `Deque<Character> st=new ArrayDeque<>(); for(char c:s.toCharArray()){ if(isOpen(c)) st.push(c); else { if(st.isEmpty() || st.pop()!=match.get(c)) return false; } } return st.isEmpty();` validates a bracketed formula.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India stores fee-calculation formulas as strings with nested grouping brackets, round for precedence, square and curly for structured sections, and a validator must confirm every bracket is balanced and correctly nested before the formula is parsed, so a malformed formula is rejected early. The validation runs on every formula edit so it must be linear. Checking valid parentheses with a stack is exactly this.

This is exactly how Valid Parentheses works in Java — pushing openers and matching each closer against the stack top.

Problem 2 — A formula might close a bracket that was never opened, or leave an opener unclosed, or cross bracket types, and all three must be rejected. This shows the empty-stack-on-closer, the non-empty-at-end, and the crossed-type failure conditions.

What the code will do: a `BracketValidator` with `isValid(String formula)` using a stack and a closer-to-opener map with the final emptiness check. The demo validates several bracketed formulas.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the fee formula `{[(1+2)*3]}`.

Step 1: we scan left to right with an empty stack. The first character is `{`, an opener, so we push it; the stack is `{`. The next is `[`, an opener, push; the stack is `{ [`. The next is `(`, an opener, push; the stack is `{ [ (`.

Step 2: the characters `1`, `+`, `2` are not brackets, so they are ignored. The next is `)`, a closer; its expected opener is `(`, and the stack top is `(`, so they match, we pop, and the stack becomes `{ [`.

Step 3: the characters `*`, `3` are ignored. The next is `]`, a closer; its expected opener is `[`, and the stack top is `[`, so they match, we pop, and the stack becomes `{`.

Step 4: the final character is `}`, a closer; its expected opener is `{`, and the stack top is `{`, so they match, we pop, and the stack becomes empty. The scan ends, the stack is empty, so the formula is valid.

Step 5: for `([)]`, after pushing `(` and `[`, the closer `)` expects `(` but the stack top is `[`, a crossed mismatch, so we return false immediately. For `((`, both openers are pushed and never closed, so at the end the stack is non-empty and the result is false.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T21:50:00Z INFO '{[(1+2)*3]}' is VALID
2026-10-26T21:50:00Z INFO Result = true
2026-10-26T21:50:00Z INFO '([)]' is INVALID
2026-10-26T21:50:00Z INFO Result = false
2026-10-26T21:50:00Z INFO '((' is INVALID
2026-10-26T21:50:00Z INFO Result = false
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: "{[(1+2)*3]}"
    │ scan chars; push openers; match closers to stack top
    ▼
  '{' push → [{] ; '[' push → [{,[] ; '(' push → [{,[,(]
  ')' top '(' match → pop → [{,[]
  ']' top '[' match → pop → [{]
  '}' top '{' match → pop → []
    │ stack empty at end?
    ▼
  valid = true   ("([)]" crossed → false ; "((" leftover → false)
    ▼
  Output: balanced yes/no
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Valid Parentheses checks whether a string of round, square, and curly brackets is balanced and properly nested, and I solve it with a stack in linear time, because balanced brackets follow a last-opened-first-closed discipline that a stack models exactly. I scan the string, push every opening bracket, and on every closing bracket I verify the stack is non-empty and its top is the exact matching opener, popping on a match and returning false immediately on any mismatch or empty stack.

Both closer failure conditions matter. An empty stack on a closer means closing a bracket that was never opened, and a wrong-kind top means the nesting is crossed, like opening a round bracket and closing it with a curly one. Only an exact-match top is popped and allowed to continue. Equally essential is the final check that the stack is empty, because leftover openers mean some brackets were never closed, which would otherwise be wrongly accepted.

I keep the matching clean with a map from each closing bracket to its expected opener, which reads clearly and extends easily to more bracket types, and I return false the instant a problem is found so invalid strings fail fast. I also note the constant-time odd-length shortcut, since a string of odd length can never balance, and that the stack grows only to the maximum nesting depth.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to validate fee-calculation formulas with nested grouping brackets before parsing them, rejecting malformed formulas early on every edit, including the crossed-type and unclosed-opener cases. Explaining the stack discipline, the two closer failure conditions, the final emptiness check, and the closer-to-opener map shows the interviewer that I understand why the stack is the right tool and have covered every failure mode.
